paper_title: Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation for Unified Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) can elicit specialized visual capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), yet jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives often introduces cross-capability gradient conflicts. Training experts independently mitigates this interference, but direct reward optimization may entangle specialized knowledge with reward-hacking biases. This paper proposes Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), which trains capability-specific experts and extracts explicit skills through reward-guided reflection. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide expert supervision while remaining unavailable to the unified student, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge without explicit skills at inference time. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED consistently outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for integrating independently acquired capabilities. Further analyses reveal interference during joint capability optimization and suggest that skill augmentation promotes more consistent expert trajectories, greater attention to task-relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise in the unified student. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/SCOPED.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across broad range of multimodal tasks (Bai et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). To further enhance their downstream multimodal capabilities, recent studies have increasingly adopted Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Yu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a) to cultivate specialized visual understanding skills through task-specific rewards, including fine-grained visual perception (Sun et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2026), visual grounding (Zhang et al., 2026), and complex multimodal reasoning (Xia et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025). These approaches have demonstrated the effectiveness of RL in improving specific aspects of visual understanding. However, learning and integrating complementary visual understanding capabilities across heterogeneous multimodal tasks remains fundamental challenge in multimodal post-training (Wei et al., 2026). straightforward approach to enhancing VLM capabilities is to jointly optimize shared policy over diverse multimodal training data (Ma et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026). However, heterogeneous training objectives can induce conflicts between capability-specific gradients, making it difficult for single policy to simultaneously acquire specialized capabilities (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). To mitigate such conflicts, recent studies instead optimize capability-specific experts independently and subsequently consolidate their acquired knowledge through knowledge distillation. In particular, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) transfers knowledge by matching teacher predictions along student-generated trajectories (Agarwal et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026), while Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) extends this paradigm to multiple capability-specific teachers, enabling shared policy to integrate complementary capabilities from different experts (Ma *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 1 Preprint. et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Nevertheless, directly aligning the predictions of expert policies does not explicitly distinguish reusable capability-level strategies from capability-specific patterns, which may include overfitting and reward-hacking behaviors inadvertently encoded in these experts. To address these challenges, we introduce Skill-DeCoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), framework that decouples capability-specific skills from expert policies to better guide multimodal post-training. First, SCOPED independently optimizes set of capability-specific experts with RL, where each expert is trained on dedicated dataset with capability-level reward objective. This independent optimization allows different experts to explore diverse solution strategies for their respective visual understanding capabilities without interference from heterogeneous training objectives. Next, to acquire complementary visual understanding capabilities, SCOPED extracts capability-specific skills from the reasoning trajectories of these experts. These skills explicitly summarize reusable solution patterns underlying successful and failed expert behaviors. We then augment each expert with its corresponding skill to provide explicit procedural guidance during reasoning, thereby reducing unnecessary or capability-irrelevant reasoning patterns that may interfere with capability learning. Finally, SCOPED applies On-Policy Distillation (OPD) to transfer the complementary capabilities from these skill-augmented experts into unified student model. Extensive experiments across eight multimodal benchmarks show that SCOPED enables compact 8B model to achieve the highest average score among the evaluated models, surpassing larger opensource and leading closed-source baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate the benefits of expert distillation and the additional contribution of skill augmentation. Further analyses reveal limitations of mixed-capability optimization, including lower training rewards than independent capability RL, weak alignment with expert-guided directions, and recurring conflicts between capability-specific gradients. We also find that skill conditioning increases trajectory consistency within each capability and directs greater attention toward task-relevant visual evidence, while the distilled student better preserves expert-induced behavior.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for specializing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under capability-specific objectives (Liu et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026). By optimizing targeted reward signals, capability-specific RL enables models to focus on the visual understanding and reasoning behaviors required by particular capability, thereby developing specialized expertise (Xiong et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025). To broaden capability coverage, recent efforts have explored jointly training shared policy across heterogeneous capabilities (Ma et al., 2025; Sarch et al., 2026). However, heterogeneous objectives can induce competing gradient signals over shared parameters, causing updates beneficial to one capability to distract the optimization direction of others (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). As result, joint optimization may restrict specialized expertise, highlighting the difficulty of simultaneously developing and consolidating heterogeneous capabilities within unified policy. Rather than jointly optimizing shared policy, knowledge distillation provides an alternative route for consolidating specialized capabilities into unified model. On-policy distillation aligns teacher supervision with student-generated trajectories, effectively mitigating distribution shift (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). Recent context-conditioned variants further enrich teacher supervision with privileged information or auxiliary context (Zhao et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). For capability integration, Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) extends this paradigm to multiple independently optimized experts, distilling their complementary capabilities into shared student along student-generated rollouts (Ma et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Nevertheless, these approaches primarily transfer expert knowledge through predictive distributions, leaving reusable reasoning patterns contained in expert trajectories largely implicit and potentially propagating noisy or over-specialized expert behaviors to the student. To externalize such implicit trajectory-level knowledge, recent studies have explored abstracting raw execution experiences into explicit skills that capture reusable solution patterns (Xin et al., 2026). Trace2Skill consolidates execution trajectories into transferable skills through hierarchical consolidation (Ni et al., 2026), while SkillRL and Skill1 construct evolving skill libraries to support skill retrieval and policy improvement (Xia et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). In multimodal reasoning, Lang2Act extracts self-emergent linguistic tools from reasoning trajectories to guide fine-grained 2 Preprint. visual understanding (Xiong et al., 2026). Skill-SD further conditions the teacher on trajectoryderived skills as privileged information during self-distillation (Wang et al., 2026). Together, these studies show that trajectory-derived skills can convert implicit execution experience into explicit and reusable guidance for subsequent model optimization. While these studies demonstrate the value of trajectory-derived skills for reusable reasoning and structured supervision, how such skills can regularize supervision from multiple independently optimized capability experts during their integration into unified VLM remains underexplored.

sections.title: 3 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: In this section, we present Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), framework for acquiring and transferring diverse set of complementary visual understanding capabilities. As illustrated in Fig. 1, SCOPED consists of two stages. First, we independently train MLLMs on different capabilities with capability-specific reward signals, allowing each model to develop expertise specialized to its target visual understanding capability (Sec. 3.1). Second, to bypass the instability of joint optimization, we abstract reward-evaluated expert trajectories into explicit skills, introducing structural information asymmetry during on-policy distillation (Sec. 3.2). Serving as privileged directional anchors, these skills regularize expert supervision, compelling the student to internalize this guidance for conflict-free consolidation. 3.1 LEARNING MLLM EXPERTISE WITH CAPABILITY-SPECIFIC REINFORCEMENT While jointly learning diverse capabilities is essential for general visual understanding, optimizing shared policy over heterogeneous data can introduce conflicting optimization signals and distract the learning process (Yu et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2026). As result, improvements in one capability may interfere with the acquisition of another. To mitigate such interference, SCOPED decouples capability learning through independent reinforcement learning, producing specialized capability experts together with reward-evaluated trajectories that capture their acquired behaviors. Eliciting Capability-Specific Expertise. For each capability c, an expert policy is initialized from the shared base policy πθ and optimized independently on Bc. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY
sections.content: This section first describes the datasets, evaluation metrics, and baselines. Then, we introduce the implementation details of our experiments. Datasets. The evaluation covers eight benchmarks across four capability groups. CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023) and PixMo-Count (Deitke et al., 2025) are used for fine-grained perception; CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c) and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) for OCR and chart understanding; VisualPuzzles (Song et al., 2025) and We-Math (Qiao et al., 2025) for symbolic visual reasoning; and MUIRBench (Wang et al., 2025a) and MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) for multiimage reasoning. For capability-specific expert training, reinforcement learning data are constructed from six public multimodal datasets, including task-relevant subsets of Orsta-Data-47K (Ma et al., 2025). Detailed dataset composition and statistics are provided in Appendix A.1. Evaluation Metrics. We employ task-specific metrics following the official evaluation protocols of each benchmark. Fine-grained perception, chart understanding, symbolic visual reasoning, and multi-image reasoning tasks are evaluated using accuracy. OCR recognition is evaluated using micro-F1 following CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c). sections.title: 5 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: In this section, we first evaluate the overall performance of SCOPED across eight multimodal benchmarks and conduct ablation studies to assess the effectiveness of its key components. We then provide in-depth analyses of cross-capability gradient interference under mixed-capability optimization and investigate how skill augmentation influences expert supervision during capability integration. 5.1 OVERALL PERFORMANCE As shown in Table 1, we report the performance of various VLMs across eight benchmarks. The evaluation results show that SCOPED consistently improves the Qwen3-VL backbone across heterogeneous visual understanding capabilities. In particular, SCOPED-8B outperforms its backbone on all eight benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 5.83 points. We adopt Qwen3-VL as the backbone due to its competitive performance across the evaluated capability groups. Nevertheless, existing models often exhibit uneven performance across different capabilities, making it challenging to simultaneously maintain strong performance in perception, OCR and chart understanding, symbolic reasoning, and multi-image reasoning. In contrast, SCOPED consistently strengthens the backbone across all four capability groups. We further apply SCOPED to Qwen3-VL-4B, where it achieves an average improvement of 3.90 points and surpasses several larger open-source models. The consistent gains observed with both the 4B and 8B backbones demonstrate that the effectiveness of SCOPED generalizes across model scales and remains robust across diverse visual capabilities. 5.2 ABLATION STUDY As shown in Table 2, we conduct ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of different multitask training strategies and the individual components of SCOPED. We first compare SCOPED with SFT and Mix-RL to assess the benefits of our training paradigm. We then ablate key components of SCOPED to examine their respective contributions. For reference, we also report the performance of capability-specific experts, each of which is optimized exclusively with task-specific rewards. The evaluation results show that SFT underperforms the zero-shot backbone, suggesting that jointly fine-tuning on capability-specific data can introduce interference across capabilities. Although MixRL improves overall performance, it still underperforms the corresponding specialized experts on symbolic visual reasoning and multi-image reasoning, indicating that joint optimization may limit the acquisition of specialized capabilities. In contrast, SCOPED achieves an average improvement of 3.82 points over Mix-RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of separating capability acquisition from capability integration. The skill-augmented expert results further show that matching each expert with its corresponding skill consistently improves the target capability, while its effects on nontarget capabilities are limited and occasionally negative. This result highlights the capability-specific nature of the extracted guidance and motivates explicit skill-expert matching during distillation. Furthermore, we compare two variants of SCOPED, SCOPED (Parameter Merging) and SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, which use parameter merging and distillation without skill augmentation, respectively, to unify multiple capability-specific experts into single model. SCOPED (Parameter Merging) consistently underperforms the on-policy distillation variants, suggesting that directly 7 Preprint. (a) Training Reward. In contrast, SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation already outperforms Mix-RL, indicating that token-level supervision from the corresponding experts along student-generated trajectories provides more fine-grained guidance for learning different capabilities. This allows the unified model to progressively absorb expertise that was independently acquired by the specialized experts. Building on this foundation, the full SCOPED framework achieves further average improvement, with gains across all four capability groups. These results indicate that explicit skills extracted from expert experience provide more targeted distillation signals, facilitating specialized capability distillation. 5.3 GRADIENT INTERFERENCE IN MULTI-CAPABILITY TRAINING As illustrated in Figure 2, we investigate the cross-capability gradient interference phenomenon (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021) during shared-policy optimization from three complementary perspectives: training reward, expert-guided update alignment, and pairwise gradient conflict. We first evaluate the training dynamics in Figure 2a. While both independent capability RL and Mix-RL steadily improve their average rewards, independent optimization maintains consistent advantage throughout most of the training process. Although the performance gap narrows toward convergence, the overall trend clearly indicates that mixed-capability optimization structurally limits the gains achievable through capability-specific learning, preventing the model from fully benefiting from independently optimized capability objectives. To uncover the mechanistic cause of this limitation, we analyze how the realized Mix-RL updates align with the behaviors acquired by independently trained capability experts. We characterize this parameter-space update alignment using cosine similarity (Xu et al., 2026b). Specifically, for each capability, we derive local expert-guided direction from the negative gradient of the KL divergence between the current Mix-RL policy and the corresponding fixed capability expert under matched response prefixes. We then compute its cosine similarity against the actual parameter displacement between adjacent Mix-RL checkpoints. In this formulation, positive values denote movement toward the expert, whereas near-zero or negative values indicate orthogonal or contradictory updates. As shown in Figure 2b, the shared updates show weak alignment with the expert-guided directions, with negative values observed across multiple capabilities and training stages. This confirms severe see-saw effect: shared-policy optimization inevitably forces trade-offs, improving certain capabilities at the direct expense of others rather than consistently approximating all capability-specific experts simultaneously. This interference is further supported by analyzing the capability-specific optimization directions themselves. At each Mix-RL checkpoint, we estimate capability-specific gradients using the corresponding capability data and compute pairwise cosine similarities among the four capabilities (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). Positive cosine similarity indicates aligned optimization directions, whereas negative values indicate that two capabilities favor opposing local updates. Figure 2c reveals recurrent negative cosine similarities across multiple capability pairs at different training stages, providing direct empirical evidence that heterogeneous capabilities can favor competing local optimization directions. Together, these results demonstrate that shared-policy optimization is constrained by cross-capability interference. These results further support the motivation of SCOPED to decouple capability acquisition into independently optimized experts prior to subsequent integration. 8 Preprint. sections.title: 5.4 EFFECTIVENESS OF SKILL-AUGMENTED DISTILLATION IN SCOPED
sections.content: In this section, we further investigate how skill augmentation regularizes expert supervision during the distillation process of SCOPED. As illustrated in Figure 3, we examine its effects from three complementary perspectives: the preservation of expert-induced behavior in the unified student, the consistency of expert trajectories across instances within each capability, and the utilization of task-relevant visual evidence. We first characterize functional capability preservation using token-level log-probability shifts relative to the base model on fixed trajectories (Klabunde et al., 2025). For each trajectory, we construct shift vector from these log-probability changes and compare the unified student with the corresponding expert in terms of amplitude retention and expert alignment. Amplitude retention quantifies how much of the expert-induced shift is preserved by the student, while expert alignment measures the cosine similarity between their shift vectors. We evaluate models distilled from different capability-specific RL experts across visual understanding capabilities. As shown in Figure 3a, SCOPED achieves higher amplitude retention and expert alignment than Mix-RL, demonstrating better preservation of expert-induced functional behavior across capabilities. Notably, SCOPED also outperforms SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, indicating that the extracted skills help the student better acquire and reconcile complementary expert capabilities. To further uncover the role of skill augmentation in SCOPED, we evaluate the consistency of expert generation by encoding reasoning trajectories produced by each capability expert with and without its corresponding skill using Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (Li et al., 2026). Within each capability, we compute pairwise cosine similarities between trajectory embeddings generated from different inputs to obtain the distributions shown in Figure 3b. Higher similarity indicates more consistent expert behavior across instances. With skill conditioning, SCOPED shifts the trajectory similarity distribution toward higher values, indicating that explicit skill guidance regularizes expert generation and promotes more consistent trajectory representations. Finally, we investigate whether this trajectory-level regularization extends to visual evidence utilization. Building on findings that attention patterns in VLMs can effectively capture task-relevant visual grounding (Kang et al., 2025), we compare each capability expert with and without its corresponding skill under identical inputs. At each decoder layer, we identify the most-attended visual token for each attention head and record hit if it falls within the task-relevant region. We then average the resulting hit rates across attention heads and evaluation samples. As shown in Figure 3c, skill-augmented experts consistently achieve higher hit rates across most of the upper decoder layers, with the largest improvement observed in the final layer. This finding indicates that explicit skills steer capability experts toward more accurate allocation of attention to task-relevant visual evidence. Taken together, these multi-level analyses suggest that skill conditioning promotes more consistent expert trajectories and more effective visual grounding, while enabling the distilled student to better preserve expert-induced functional behavior. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: This paper proposes SCOPED, aiming at integrating complementary visual understanding capabilities into unified Vision-Language Model through skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. SCOPED independently optimizes capability-specific experts and abstracts reusable solution patterns from reward-evaluated trajectories into explicit capability skills. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide capability experts to provide structured supervision for the unified student. Our experiments demonstrate that SCOPED consistently improves performance across diverse visual understanding capabilities. Our further analyses reveal cross-capability interference during mixedcapability optimization and show that skill augmentation improves the preservation and transfer of specialized expert capabilities.

Finegrained visual perception is assessed using CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023) and PixMoCount (Deitke et al., 2025). OCR and chart understanding are evaluated on the recognition track of CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c) and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022). Symbolic visual reasoning is evaluated on VisualPuzzles (Song et al., 2025) and We-Math (Qiao et al., 2025). Multi-image reasoning is evaluated on MUIRBench (Wang et al., 2025a) and MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025). Table 3 summarizes the evaluation scale and primary capability of each benchmark. As shown in Table 6, SFT substantially underperforms the zero-shot backbone, while Mix-RL yields only modest overall improvement and remains below the corresponding capability-specific experts on several target capabilities. In contrast, independently trained experts achieve stronger performance on their respective capabilities, showing that the benefit of separating capability acquisition from integration remains evident with smaller backbone. The skill-augmented expert results exhibit trend consistent with Qwen3-VL-8B. Conditioning each expert on its matched skill improves performance on the corresponding target capability, while the effects on non-target capabilities remain limited or mixed. A.5 SKILL CONSTRUCTION DETAILS We provide additional implementation details for the capability-wise skill abstraction procedure introduced in Sec. 3.2. Skill construction uses only training data and training-set rollouts, while the held-out evaluation set is used exclusively for final evaluation. For each capability, single skill is constructed from the trajectories generated by its corresponding optimized expert. Trajectory Curation. For each training instance, the optimized capability expert samples multiple rollout trajectories, each of which is evaluated by the corresponding capability-specific reward function. To reduce redundancy, we deduplicate repeated trajectories within each task subtype and balance the retained trajectories across subtypes so that high-resource tasks do not dominate the subsequent skill construction process. Reward-Based Trajectory Grouping. Following Sec. 3.2, the curated trajectories are divided into successful and failed cohorts according to their capability-specific rewards. This grouping provides complementary evidence about effective solution patterns and recurring failure modes. Trajectory-Level Reflection. The optimized capability expert performs trajectory-level reflection over the successful and failed cohorts using outcome-specific reflection prompts. Successful trajectories are used to identify reusable solution strategies and verification behaviors, while failed trajectories are analyzed to diagnose recurring failure mechanisms and derive corrective guidance. The resulting reflections are aggregated into capability-specific evidence ledger containing both effective behaviors and failure-avoidance guidance. Capability Skill Synthesis. Based on the aggregated trajectory-derived evidence, the same capability expert synthesizes single capability-level skill containing reusable procedural guidance for the corresponding capability. The resulting skill is subsequently used to condition the expert during skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. This procedure produces one skill for each of the four capabilities. Detailed reflection and skill-induction prompts are provided in Appendix A.12. Ablation of Trajectory Sources. A.12 PROMPT EXAMPLES We provide the prompt templates used for both skill construction and evaluation. Skill Construction Prompts. Our skill construction procedure uses three main prompts. First, the successful-trajectory self-reflection prompt asks the optimized capability expert to identify reusable verification behaviors and their activation conditions from its successful trajectories. Second, the failed-trajectory self-reflection prompt asks the same expert to diagnose causal failure mechanisms and derive corresponding corrective principles. Finally, the evidence-grounded skill induction prompt provides the curated evidence ledger to the same expert and asks it to consolidate recurring success and failure patterns into compact capability-level skill. The corresponding prompt templates are shown in Figures 1113. Evaluation Prompts. Figure 14 presents the vanilla evaluation prompt, where the model receives the input image(s), the benchmark-specific query, and the corresponding response instruction. The model is instructed to reason step by step and place its final response within <answer> and </answer> tags. For evaluating skill-augmented capability experts in the ablation and analysis experiments, we preserve the original multimodal input and response instruction and condition each expert on its corresponding capability skill. The four extracted skills correspond to perception, OCR and chart understanding, symbolic reasoning, and multi-image reasoning, respectively.
